signals.source_text: In 1936, Sarla Thakral became the first Indian woman to earn a pilot's licence. Ninety years later, her photograph hangs on our wall, and the company that carries her name is building India's electric air taxi. For the first chapter of Women in Aviation @ Sarla, we sat down with six of the women designing and building it. They spoke about being one of five or six women in an aerospace engineering class. They spoke about growing up in a tier two city where no one knew a career in aviation was possible, and about why so few women stay in core technology roles. And they spoke about what it takes to design an aircraft, which one of them compared to raising a child: every structure, every sub-component, every detail from birth. What stayed with all of them was Sarla herself. As one of them put it, "She walked the path so that we can run on it." Thank you to Vijeta Tantry , Payal Satish , Nishtha Sharma , Pavana Prabhu , Saisurya Anbazhagan Vanniyar and Medha Deshpande for sharing your stories. #WomenInAviation #SarlaAviation #eVTOL #Aerospace

signals.source_text: I'm so thankful I caught the tail end of the glory days of aviation. There was a time when stepping onto a plane meant something, when the flight deck held a full crew and flying still carried a sense of adventure, romance, and ceremony. My generation wants to believe pilotless cockpits will never happen, but I think that's just our Gen X mindset talking. We came of age when the three-person flight deck was still a thing (captain, first officer, flight engineer) and watched, in real time, as that number got whittled down to two. We know firsthand how essential that third set of eyes and hands was, right up until the airlines decided it wasn't. And here's the uncomfortable part: within a generation, it felt normal that two pilots were enough. So when I insist "they'll never get rid of the second pilot," I have to ask: isn't that exactly what someone in the three-pilot era would have said about the flight engineer? Am I still a realist by treating the two-pilot cockpit as sacred, or am I being nostalgic, mistaking the last configuration I personally lived through for a natural limit rather than just another checkpoint on a long trend line toward fewer pilots, and eventually, however uncomfortable it is to say, none at all... https://lnkd.in/gQQM9D68 Joby Aviation #aviation #history #aviationhistory #pilot #pilottraining #fly #flight #information #conversation #discussion #achickinthecockpit #pilotlife #airlines #airplane #aircraft #autonomous #engineering #innovation #learn #

signals.source_text: There are words and expressions that are bandied about - “safe” and “fully-qualified” come to mind - that are poorly understood, IMHO. In re the first word - “safe” - I believe that there are such things as more-safe and less-safe; I don’t believe there exists anything that is completely-safe. And people make decisions about activities using an internal judgment of “safe enough.” We drive cars toward other cars with a combined velocity of over 100 mph, divided by a yellow stripe or a dashed white line painted on the highway surface. We have very little idea what is happening in the other vehicle - screaming kids, teenagers texting, and worse…and yet we consider it safe enough. “Fully-qualified” is another expression used to describe, in this context, the two current occupants of an airline cockpit. People, understandably, assume that the FAA is making sure that the airline is making sure that the simulator instructors are making sure that the new pilot - captain or first officer - is “fully-qualified.” How would we describe these pilots after years in real world airline operations - “Way-qualified?” “Outrageously-qualified?” (There's more, which I'll add in a reply to this comment.)

signals.source_text: Great Splash Singapore event! “Strategy is no longer about predicting the future; it’s about building optionality for different futures.” This takeaway of SPLASH Singapore strongly resonates with the challenge of decarbonising shipping. With the future fuel mix still uncertain, the answer may not be to bet everything on a single fuel today. It may also be about reducing our dependence on any fuel. This is precisely where wind-assisted propulsion can make a difference: by harnessing a renewable energy source that is available today and independent of the fuel used on board. By reducing a vessel’s energy demand, wind assistance can help: - Limit exposure to fuel prices and availability; - Mitigate long-term technology risks; - Improve the performance of multiple fuel pathways; - Preserve flexibility in an uncertain regulatory environment. Wind-assisted propulsion is therefore more than a decarbonisation solution. It is also a way to build strategic optionality. In an uncertain future, could one of the smartest choices simply be to need less fuel—whatever that fuel may be? #Maritime #Shipping #WindAssistedPropulsion #Decarbonisation #EnergyTransition #SPLASHSingapore

signals.source_text: Иногда на собеседовании можно удивить даже Senior-разработчика. Примерно полгода назад проходил собеседование на позицию Backend Developer внутри Сбера. Разговор зашёл о Kafka и consumer groups. Обсуждали ситуацию, когда одна consumer group читает несколько топиков. А точнее вред такого подхода. Я упомянул интересный нюанс: ошибка или нестабильность consumer'а, возникшая при работе с одним топиком, может привести к rebalance и повлиять на обработку других топиков той же consumer group. С подобным я сталкивался на практике. Вал ошибок, который ни с того ни с сего возник при вычитке топика, который давно никто не трогал, был связан как раз с такой проблемой. Собеседующий сначала не поверил и подумал, что я что-то путаю. Он был уверен, что ребалансировка не может выходить за пределы одного топика. В итоге я оказался прав.🕺😁 Для меня это был хороший пример того, что собеседование не только проверяет твои знания. Иногда ты сам можешь принести на интервью что-то новое для собеседующего.
